claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites are susceptible to phase separation and interfacial void formation under thermal and irradiation stress.
A nanoscale, conformal Ti or Cr interlayer can be deposited at W/Cu interfaces before or during consolidation.
A Ti or Cr interlayer will chemically stabilize the W/Cu junction during processing.
The interlayer will suppress phase-separated regions at the W/Cu interface under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The interlayer will suppress interfacial void formation under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Relevant service conditions include heat fluxes of tens of MW/m² and fusion-relevant neutron irradiation.
The Ti or Cr interlayer is likely to form thermally and irradiation-stable intermetallic compounds at the W/Cu interface.
The stabilized interfacial region mitigates diffusion gradients.
Mitigating diffusion gradients suppresses void nucleation.
Ti or Cr chemically bonds with both W and Cu.
Chemical bonding by the interlayer reduces the driving force for phase separation and void formation.
Enhanced interfacial stability produces a more continuous thermal-conduction path.
A more continuous thermal path sustains higher thermal conductivity under harsh service conditions.
Under identical exposure conditions, interlayer-treated W–Cu will have fewer voids and a more homogeneous interface than untreated W–Cu.
Interlayer-treated W–Cu will exhibit significantly improved and sustained thermal conductivity relative to untreated W–Cu.
Interfacial void formation and phase separation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu over time.
An excessively thick interlayer may limit the intervention's effectiveness.
Formation of undesirable brittle interfacial phases may limit the intervention's effectiveness.
